analysis.one_liner: Bans clearcutting on federal lands and protects old-growth, roadless, and watershed forests from logging.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 1997 by Senator Torricelli with five Democratic cosponsors, was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and its forests subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Act to Save America's Forests would have banned clearcutting and other even-age logging on all federal forest lands — national forests, public lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management, wildlife refuges, Indian lands, and military lands. It would also have barred logging and road building in old-growth 'Ancient Forests', roadless areas, land along streams and lakes, and dozens of named special areas across 26 states. And it would have let any citizen sue to enforce those rules, with damages and attorney's fees, including suing the federal government itself.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public: the bill's stated purposes were conserving native biodiversity, protecting drinking-water watersheds, fish and wildlife habitat, and recreation, and ending federal logging programs its findings described as running at a large cost to taxpayers. People who hunt, fish, hike, and depend on clean water from federal forests were the intended beneficiaries, as were endangered species and the small towns whose recreation and fishing economies the bill said were being damaged by logging and roadbuilding.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited even-age logging — clearcutting, seed-tree cutting, and shelterwood cutting — across every forested stand and watershed on federal lands, requiring a shift to selective logging or ecological restoration.

It barred road construction and logging in Ancient Forests, Roadless Areas, Watershed Protection Areas, Special Areas, and Federal Boundary Areas, naming protected areas in 26 states from Alabama to Wyoming.

It gave any citizen harmed by a violation the right to sue in federal court — including against the United States, whose sovereign immunity the bill waived — with a minimum $5,000 damage award, injunctions, and attorney's fees.

Its findings stated that less than 10 percent of the nation's original unlogged forests remain, most on federal land, and that logging there costs the Treasury and taxpayers enormously while damaging fisheries, recreation, and water supplies.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which buys federal timber: the bill would have sharply reduced the volume and methods of logging on national forests and other federal lands, eliminated clearcutting entirely, and closed designated areas to logging and road construction. Logging-dependent mill towns and contractors could bear reduced federal timber sales, though the bill argued selective logging is more job-intensive per unit of timber produced.

drawbacks.text: Restricting logging to selective methods and closing large designated areas would reduce the federal timber supply, which the timber industry and communities with mills built around federal sales would feel as lost volume and revenue — a cost the bill acknowledged by arguing that selection logging is more labor-intensive per amount of timber, but which it did not quantify.

The bill permanently designated dozens of named special areas by statute, from the Sipsey Wilderness to a 500,000-acre North Rim of the Grand Canyon area, removing land-management flexibility for federal agencies and future Congresses regardless of changing forest conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — protecting the last remnants of old-growth forest, drinking-water watersheds, fisheries, and recreation, while ending timber sales its own findings described as costly to taxpayers — were broad and durable, and ordinary citizens would have gained new enforcement tools. The costs fall on a concentrated timber industry and on some logging-dependent communities, and the selective-logging requirement would have been more expensive per board foot than clearcutting. The design was prescriptive and rigid, but the trade it offered was public lands protection in exchange for lower federal timber output.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in June 1997, the bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and then to its forests subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote ever took place, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Torricelli introduced the Act to Save America's Forests on June 27, 1997, joined by Senator Kerry, and five Democratic senators cosponsored it.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day it was introduced.
Three days later, on June 30, 1997, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Forests and Public Lands — the last action the bill ever received.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies and logging operations that rely on federal timber sales are better off, because clearcutting and road building on national forests and other federal lands continued without the bill's restrictions. The bill's findings stated these federal logging programs operated at a large financial cost to taxpayers, so that subsidy also continued.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Joined Torricelli in introducing the bill

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired in the 105th Congress by Frank Murkowski of Alaska)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Forests and Public Lands on June 30, 1997 and never held a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee

against.name: Timber industry
against.role: Buyers of federal timber sales and logging operators on national forests and BLM land
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on clearcutting and logging on federal lands, which would have cut off a substantial share of their timber supply

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired Energy Committee never acted on the bill; there were no votes, so the partisan split was never formally tested.

industries.note: The bill banned clearcutting and other even-age logging on national forests, BLM land, refuges, Indian lands, and military lands, and closed named areas to logging and road construction, sharply cutting the federal timber available to the industry. Its interest in the bill ran against the public benefits of forest and watershed protection the bill was written to secure.

The bill's findings said destruction of large unfragmented forests had cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, recreation, and guiding, and that protected forests would sustain those economies alongside the public's recreation and clean-water interests.

industries.industry: Federal land management agencies (Forest Service, BLM, Fish and Wildlife Service, Defense Department)
industries.note: The bill imposed binding biodiversity duties on these agencies, restricted their timber programs, and exposed them to citizen lawsuits with waived sovereign immunity, while giving scientists rather than agency insiders a formal advisory role.
